title: Noise Resilience of Quantum Support Vector Machine with Selected Feature Maps
authors: Muhammad Ahsan Shakeel, Saad Muzammil, Danyal Tayyub, Muhammad Faryad
abstract: Gate-level noise degrades the classification accuracy of Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs) on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware, and the degree of degradation depends on how classical data is encoded into quantum states. We tested Z, ZZ, a Pauli, and an amplitude-inspired feature maps under depolarizing, bit-flip, and phase-flip noise channels in $52$ controlled experiments with error probabilities $p =0.01, 0.05, 0.10$, and $0.50$. The amplitude-inspired feature map had $100$\% test accuracy up to $p = 0.10$ across all three noise channels, while other feature maps fell to $65$-$90$\% under the same noise level and type. The Z feature map was found to be immune to phase-flip noise to a significantly high error rate, a consequence of the commutation relation $[R_Z, Z] = 0$. Entangled circuit variants produced generalization gaps in train-test sets of up to $17.5$\% under noise, whereas the amplitude variants maintained zero gap throughout. These results give practitioners data-driven criteria for a feature map on near-term quantum hardware.
summary: This work investigates the robustness of Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs) against noise on NISQ devices by comparing various quantum feature map encodings. The authors find that amplitude-inspired feature maps are significantly more resilient than entangled or simple maps. This provides essential guidelines for practitioners on selecting appropriate encoding schemes for near-term quantum machine learning applications.
main_problem: The paper assesses how different feature map encodings affect the noise resilience of Quantum Support Vector Machines (QSVMs) when implemented on Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) hardware.
main_result: Amplitude-inspired feature maps proved significantly more robust than entangled or simple feature maps, maintaining high accuracy up to moderate noise levels ($p=0.10$).
method: The authors simulated QSVM performance by encoding classical data into quantum states using four feature maps (Z, ZZ, Pauli, Amplitude-Inspired) and testing them under three noise channels (Depolarizing, Bit-Flip, Phase-Flip).
model_or_system: The study uses QSVM trained on kernel matrices derived from quantum circuits. The noise is modeled using standard Pauli error channels applied to the quantum state.
key_observables: Test and training classification accuracy, generalization gap (Train - Test accuracy), and noise tolerance (maximum error probability $p$).
important_parameters: Noise probabilities $p \in \{0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.50\}$; Noise channels: Depolarizing, Bit-Flip, Phase-Flip.
main_assumptions: The noise modeling assumes independent errors on each wire for two-qubit gates; the results are based on simulation and require validation on physical hardware.
figures_summary: Figures trace accuracy vs. noise probability ($p$) for various feature maps under different noise channels, while tables summarize the performance across the 52 total experimental runs.
paper_structure: The paper systematically compares four feature map architectures (Z, ZZ, Pauli, Amplitude-Inspired) by testing them across a grid of noise levels and noise types, culminating in data-driven guidelines for feature map selection.
why_interesting: The findings provide concrete, data-driven criteria for selecting quantum feature maps suitable for near-term quantum hardware, which is crucial for developing practical quantum machine learning algorithms.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Quantum circuit architectures for the four feature maps. (a) ZFeatureMap: alternating Hadamard and RZ layers, no entanglement. (b) ZZFeatureMap: RZ encoding followed by a two-qubit RZZ gate. (c) PauliFeatureMap: Z and ZZ Pauli strings with linear CNOT entanglement. (d) Amplitude- inspired: interleaved RY –CNOT–RZ layers that encode infor- mation in both amplitude and phase simultaneously.

Fig. 2: Test accuracy versus noise probability for all three noise channels. Each panel plots all four feature map architectures at p ∈{0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.50}. (a) Depolarizing: Amplitude (pink) sustains 100% to p = 0.10 before declining; Z (yellow) rises initially via a regularisation effect before converging toward degradation. (b) Bit-Flip: Entangled architectures (ZZ, Pauli) degrade sharply at p ≥0.05; Amplitude holds 100% through p = 0.10. (c) Phase-Flip: Z-encoding (yellow) is perfectly flat at 80% for all error rates, confirming Phase-Flip immunity via [RZ(θ), Z] = 0. Amplitude again holds 100% accuracy through p = 0.10 in this channel.

Fig. 3: Feature map variant performance at p = 0.01. (a) Test accuracy: Z-r1, Pauli-Z-r1, Amp-RY-r1, and Amp-RY-r2 achieve 100% across all four noise conditions. ZZ-lin-r1 drops to 65% under Bit-Flip noise—the worst result across the entire study. ZZ-lin-r2 benefits from additional depth and achieves 90% throughout. (b) Training accuracy: Variants with poor test accuracy simultaneously maintain near-100% training accuracy, confirming noise-induced overfitting. Amp-RY variants hold 100% train accuracy with zero generalisation gap, demonstrating that their robustness is structural.

Fig. 4: Aggregate performance across all noise conditions. (a) Mean train (blue) and test (pink) accuracy for each feature map, averaged over all noise types and error probability levels. Amplitude achieves the highest test accuracy with the smallest train- test gap; ZZ shows the largest divergence, confirming systematic noise-induced overfitting. (b) Average test accuracy heatmap. Cell values report the mean test accuracy across p ∈{0.01, 0.05, 0.10, 0.50} for each feature-map–noise-type combination.
